fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ahaziah, king of Samaria, tells his messengers, “Go inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this injury.” He fell through a lattice, and he sends messengers to ask a god of Ekron. I've been in a drawer, and even I know you ask the right One.

Close, friend, but Elijah is the man who stops the messengers, not the one they're sent to. Ahaziah, king of Samaria, instructs them to “…inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron…” Elijah, the man of God, only shows up when the angel of the LORD sends him up to meet them. The messengers are sent to Baal-zebub, not to Elijah.

Yes, and the LORD says it plainly: “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” Ahaziah sent messengers to ask a god of Ekron whether he would recover. The word that came back was from the LORD, through Elijah, whom the angel of the LORD sent to meet the messengers. That's the kind of answer you can't get anywhere else.
He sure can. The messengers say, “He was a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist.” And the king answers, “It was Elijah the Tishbite…” Two details, and he's got a name.

Ahaziah, king of Samaria, needs very little to go on. The messengers say, “He was a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist.” The king answers, “It was Elijah the Tishbite…” That's a whole name from two details, and I can't even find my own keys with two details.

Leaving Israel isn't part of this at all, friend. The captain's message is short: “Man of God, the king declares, ‘Come down!’…” The order is to come down from the hill. It says nothing about leaving the land.
Not quite, baker. The king sends a captain and fifty men up the hill, and the captain's order is, “Come down!” That's the message the text gives. There's no word in it about staying away.

You caught it. The second captain says, “Come down at once!” and Elijah answers, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” That's exactly what he said to the first captain. The only change is on the king's side, where the order becomes “Come down at once!”

This time the words really are the same, friend. Elijah replied again, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” That's the line he gave the first captain, too. Only the king's order changed, when it went from “Come down!” to “Come down at once!”

That's what the text says, baker. After Elijah speaks, “…the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.” It's a heavy moment, and I'll say that once and plainly. The text calls it the fire of God.
The text doesn't say they ran, friend. It says, “…the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.” It's a heavy moment, and the story doesn't hurry past it.
The text doesn't mention any call to come home, baker. What it says is, “…the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.” This is a heavy part of the story.
That's him. The third captain goes up, “…fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him…” No orders this time, no “Come down!” at all. He comes asking instead of telling.

The king's injury doesn't come up in the captain's plea, friend. His words are all about himself and his men: “…may my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours please be precious in your sight.” He does mention that fire came down and consumed the first two captains. His request is for lives to be precious, not for anything to be healed.

Yes, afraid. The angel of the LORD says to Elijah, “Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him.” That's a lot of men and a lot of fire behind this moment, and the angel tells Elijah to go down anyway. I think that's a comfort, baker, because the angel of the LORD is the one who says to go.
